notes.title: Introduction to RCS
notes.content: The Revision Control System (RCS) is an early version control tool used to track file revisions, commonly used in Unix environments before Git and SVN.

notes.title: RCS Directory Setup
notes.content: RCS stores its metadata in an RCS subdirectory. To use RCS, you must create this directory with 'mkdir RCS'. Never manually edit its contents.

notes.title: Basic Workflow
notes.content:
1. Create or edit a file.
2. Check the file in with 'ci'.
3. Retrieve it with 'co' when needed.
4. Use 'rlog' to view revision history and 'rcsdiff' to compare revisions.

notes.title: Important Commands
notes.content: ci (check in), co (check out), rcsdiff (compare versions), rlog (view history), ident (show embedded IDs). Options like -l (lock), -u (unlock), and -r (specify revision) are frequently used.

notes.title: RCS Keywords
notes.content: RCS supports embedded keywords like $Id$ that expand when files are checked in or out. These are useful for embedding version information directly in source files.

notes.title: RCS Limitations
notes.content: RCS is file-based, not repository-based, which makes it unsuitable for large multi-file projects. Modern systems like Git are preferred, but RCS principles remain foundational.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the 'ci' command in RCS?
options: Check in a file to the repository
Check out a file from the repository
quiz.explanation: 'ci' is used to check in files, creating a new revision in RCS.

quiz.question: Which RCS command compares two revisions of a file?
quiz.explanation: 'rcsdiff' is used to show differences between two versions of a file.

quiz.question: What happens when you run 'co -l filename'?
options: Checks the file in and locks it
Checks the file out and locks it for editing
quiz.explanation: 'co -l' checks out the file and locks it so others cannot modify it until checked back in.
